overview: ISSB means Inter Services Selection Board. It selects officers for the Pakistan Army, Navy and Air Force.
A 30-minute essay is written on the first day at ISSB.
Interviews at ISSB check your behaviour, thinking and personality, not only your knowledge.
Before ISSB, the initial test at the selection centre also has short essays (one English, one Urdu) and an initial interview.
Batches report to a centre (for example Kohat or Gujranwala) for about five days of tests.
Each candidate is given a chest number and is called by it during the tests.

The psychologist's test material (written psych tests, including self-description and merits/demerits) is put in your dossier and checked by the psychologist; one source says about 40% of the recommendation depends on it.
The psychologist's written tests at ISSB include OPI (personality test), word association (WAT), English and Urdu sentence completion, situation reaction, picture stories and pointer stories.
Malir (Karachi) is one of the ISSB centres; candidates there reported the full set of psychological tests, Deputy President interview, lecturette, group discussions and essay.
ISSB is not a competition between candidates; each person is judged on his own performance.
Psychological tests at ISSB include Word Association Test, Sentence Completion (English and Urdu), Picture Story, Pointer Story, Situation Reaction Test, OPI (personality questionnaire) and an essay.
Psychological tests include WAT, SCT (English and Urdu), SRT, pointer stories, picture stories and a personality (OPI) questionnaire, all assessed by the psychologist.
The Deputy President takes a personal interview.
Group discussion is the first group activity at ISSB, where candidates meet as a group for the first time.
Sources differ on who runs the group discussion: some say the Deputy President, others say the GTO, who also gives chest numbers and a group letter (like G, B or H).
The GTO (Group Testing Officer) runs the outdoor tasks on Day 3 and Day 4. Most are group tasks; only the individual obstacles are done alone.
Group Planning (Military Planning) is the first GTO exercise, so it sets the tone for all the GTO tests.
Lecturette and group discussion (GD) are indoor GTO tasks; topics usually come from current affairs, social issues, Pakistan's problems, religion, education, youth and defence.
ISSB (Inter Services Selection Board) selects young men and women who can complete officer training at the military academies and later lead soldiers in peace and war.
ISSB tests candidates for all three services: Army, Navy and Air Force. Each Service Headquarters decides how many candidates it needs for each course.
ISSB centres include Kohat, Gujranwala, Malir (Karachi) and Quetta.
Selection uses a three-part (three dimensional) system: psychological tests, GTO (Group Testing Officer) tasks and the interview.
Three specialists assess you: the Psychologist, the Group Testing Officer (GTO) and the Deputy President (interviewing officer).
Testing and interviews last about four days after the day of arrival. Recommended and other candidates leave in the afternoon of the last day.
Candidates who are screened out after the intelligence tests go home the next day of arrival at around 11 am.
There is no fixed number of candidates selected from a batch. If all meet the standard, all can be recommended; if none do, none are.
Being recommended by ISSB does not guarantee joining the academy. ISSB only recommends; the service makes the final merit list based on vacancies.
The assessment system is the same for all three services. For some courses candidates are tested in only two parts (psychologist tests and interview).
Female candidates are normally tested in psychological tests, interview and some GTO tasks, except some categories (like GD(P)) who do all tests.
You must wait at least 120 days between two ISSB appearances, and you get a limited number of chances (usually two) for a type of entry.

If you fall ill and miss all tests you are marked 'Withdrawn' and the chance is not counted. If you miss part of GTO or interview you may be 'Not Fully Boarded'; the chance is not counted and the 120-day rule does not apply.
ISSB discourages coaching academies because coached candidates show copied, stereotyped behaviour and lose their natural originality.
ISSB is a 'Selection Board', not a 'Rejection Board'. Its aim is to find the qualities of a good officer in you.
Any sifarish (influence), unfair means or not following Board instructions will disqualify you.
Call letters are sent about 20 days before the test. If you did not get the letter but your name is on the online call-up list, print that page and report with your original documents.
If your test date clashes with an exam, you can apply by post with a copy of the exam schedule for a re-call; ISSB is not bound to call you again.
Report before 3 pm on your call date. Late candidates are normally not accepted.

Free food and lodging are provided. Laundry and barber services are available on payment. Travelling allowance (equal to bus or train fare from your home address) is paid before you leave. Serving soldiers get a railway warrant from their unit instead.
ISSB Gujranwala is about 7 km from Rahwali check post on GT Road; ISSB buses run from the Garrison MP check post (around 1:00 pm to 1:45 pm).
ISSB Malir is about 5 km from Malir Halt station; buses run from Karachi Cantt railway station for out-station candidates (around 1:00 pm to 1:45 pm).

dos: Be truthful and honest in every test and interview; do not bluff.
Know your own personal, family and academic details fully.
Know Pakistan well: borders, history, armed forces and current affairs.
Keep calm and confident when stressful or awkward questions are asked.
Stay positive and natural.
Be yourself; do not copy others or try to compete with them.
Practice all psychological tests at home before going to ISSB.
Be neat: clean, well-fitting simple dress, proper haircut and shave; walk with good posture.
Be honest, straightforward and frank.
Listen carefully to every instruction; ask doubts before the test starts.
Stay calm under pressure and work fast but accurately.
Take part willingly in every activity and cooperate with others.
Know clearly why you want to join the armed forces.
Keep up with current affairs and defence matters; read good newspapers.
Improve your English and Urdu expression and vocabulary; join debates.
Take part in sports and positions of responsibility before ISSB.
Do physical exercise for weeks before reporting.
Eat only clean food while travelling to ISSB to avoid illness.
Admit your weaknesses honestly; they may count in your favour.
Females: wear respectable dress, tie hair neatly, keep nails trimmed.
Keep a positive attitude every day; treat it as a habit like exercise.
Set clear goals, break them into small steps and work on them at least 15 minutes daily.
Write your goals on paper and review them regularly.
Tell trusted people about your plans so they keep you accountable.
Reward yourself for small successes and keep a record of what you have achieved.
donts: Do not lie or make up stories about yourself.
Do not get angry or upset by tricky personal questions; they test your composure.
Do not waste time; every test has a strict time limit.
Do not copy answers or stories from books; they show the author's personality, not yours.
Do not treat ISSB as a race against other candidates.
Do not try sifarish or unfair means.
Do not bring cameras, audio-visual items, knives, firearms, pets, drugs, banned items, valuables or large sums of money. Mobile phones are deposited at reception.
Do not leave ISSB premises during your stay.
Do not be rash or aggressive, and do not be dull or spiritless.
Do not show off, bluff or give a false picture of yourself.
Do not get nervous or frightened.
Do not ask other candidates about instructions during a test.
Do not wear jewellery during obstacles/tasks.
Do not rely on coaching-centre stock answers.
Do not lose heart if not recommended; it only means another career may suit you better.
Do not expect to change your whole personality overnight; improve one or two traits at a time.
Do not dwell on negative thoughts or self-pity.
Do not take every criticism personally; check if it is true, fix it if it is, ignore it if it is not.
Do not make excuses for fear; recognise it honestly.
Do not babble or talk too much about yourself.
Do not quarrel, use bad language or make sarcastic remarks.
Do not be selfish, individualistic or stay aloof from the group.
Do not bluff or try to cheat the board; they are experienced officers.
Do not look over-serious or tense.
Do not try to copy someone else; be yourself.

Day 1: Written psychological tests are done in the hall: essay (30 minutes), Word Association Test, Situation Reaction Test, English and Urdu sentence completion, personality questionnaire (OPI), picture stories and pointer stories.
Arrival day (before this): report before 3 pm, documents checked, photograph taken, fill the Board Questionnaire / PIQ (bio-data).
Opening address by the Deputy President.
Remaining psychological tests (WAT, SCT, picture story, self description etc.). Screened-out candidates do not attend further tests.

Fill the biodata form, which includes writing about one given life event (e.g. 'Aim of my life' or 'Happiest day of my life').
Day 2: Group tests start: group discussion (English and Urdu topics) and lecturette.
Psychological tests are normally held on Day 2: Word Association, Sentence Completion, Picture Story Writing, then Pointer Story Writing.
Sentence completion: two English sets of 26 (6 minutes each) and two Urdu sets of 26 (6 minutes each).
Pointer Story: two incomplete 2-line stories, each shown for 30 seconds, then 30 seconds to think and 3.5 minutes to write.

Psychological tests: word association, English and Urdu sentence completion, pointer stories, situation reaction test (10 situations), OPI (about 150 statements in 50 minutes) and picture stories (4 pictures, about 4 minutes each).
Indoor tasks: Group Discussion and Group Planning.
Outdoor tasks: Progressive Group Task (PGT) and Half Group Task (HGT).
Wake up at Fajr, pray, get ready; breakfast after about 30-40 min.
Day 3: Interviews with Deputy President, psychologist and GTO happen during the stay (Deputy interview may be on any day).
Group discussions in English and Urdu, lecturette and other GTO tasks.
GTO outdoor tasks begin, starting with Group (Military) Planning.
Wake at Fajr, breakfast, wear neat clothes and go to the test hall.
GTOs come in one by one and call chest numbers; your group forms and you get a new GTO chest number, and the group gets a letter (e.g. A, G, T).
GTO takes the group to a room for indoor tasks: introduction, Group Discussion, Lecturette, Group Planning.
Change into tracksuit and wait in Nishtar Hall until called.
Outdoor tasks in the task area: Progressive Group Task (PGT) and Half/Semi Group Task (HGT).
Day 4: Remaining GTO outdoor tasks continue, including individual obstacles and command task.
Candidates are dispersed (sent home) in the afternoon.
Wake at Fajr, breakfast, wear tracksuit and go to the test hall.
Instructions on individual obstacles shown on multimedia.
Wait in Nishtar Hall/cabin; each candidate does the individual obstacles alone when the whistle blows.
The group then goes with the GTO for the Command Task, Final Group Task (FGT) and Mutual Assessment.
Lunch around 1 pm, free time; photos are delivered in the afternoon.
Day 5: Wake at Fajr, breakfast, change dress and pack your things.
No tests except re-interviews: gather in the lawn; some chest numbers are called for re-interview (or conference).
Collect mobile phones and travel allowance (TA).
The ISSB bus drops you at the bus stop; result comes later by courier.
Departure Day: Fajr, breakfast, pack your things and pay the washerman.
No tests, except for candidates called for a re-interview; wait in the lawn until the helper calls chest numbers.
Collect your mobile phone and travel allowance (TA). The ISSB bus drops you at the bus stop.
Result is sent later by courier.
Departure Day: final interview with the Deputy President, re-interviews, re-command task or re-obstacles for some candidates, then departure.

Screening has three parts: verbal MCQs, non-verbal MCQs (shapes, figures, sequences) and mechanical aptitude.

Practise quick mental maths: speed-distance, eggs/dozen, ratio, zakat (2.5%), poles, percentage, income and averages. Try to answer in 6-10 seconds without paper.

10 situations, about 2 minutes each (20 minutes total), shown on screen; write reactions on an answer sheet.

items.s: An injured man is lying on the road; people say he is a thief and his condition is serious.
items.r: Gave him first aid, took him to hospital and informed the police.

items.s: Your friend left school because of daily quarrels between his parents.
items.r: Encouraged him, helped with studies and asked elders to talk to his parents so he could rejoin school.

items.s: You committed a sin. If you ask for forgiveness openly you will be defamed in society; if you stay quiet, everything goes well.
items.r: Sincerely repent to Allah, make up for the wrong if anyone was harmed, and never repeat it.

items.s: Your uncle paid your fees when your father could not, and now asks you to marry his daughter whom you do not like.
items.r: Thank him with respect, and politely and honestly explain my feelings with my parents' help; I repay his favour in other ways.

items.s: A friend is taking sleeping pills without a doctor because of home and money problems.
items.r: Stop him gently, take him to a doctor, inform his family and help him find a way through his problems.

items.s: Someone you know robbed a bank and gave all the money to the poor.
items.r: Report it to the police; good aims do not justify crime, and I help the poor in legal ways.

items.s: Your job sends you on an important mission but your family refuses permission due to family problems.
items.r: Calm my family, arrange support for their problem through relatives, and go on the mission as duty comes first.

items.s: Your younger sister is modern and your parents want her to marry an older man; she does not agree.
items.r: Talk calmly with parents, share her view, and look for a suitable match agreed by all.

items.s: You are alone in a room with a girl you like.
items.r: Behave respectfully, keep the door open and leave; respect her honour.

items.s: You got a recommendation letter; to whom would you give it in your group (son of a martyr, boy whose mother is in hospital, or yourself)?
items.r: Keep it myself, since it is earned on merit, and support the others in other ways.

items.s: Parents want you to marry your cousin but you like someone else.
items.r: Discuss respectfully with parents and reach a decision together.

items.s: You love a girl and later learn she belongs to another sect.
items.r: Sect is no barrier to a good person; decide with families' consent.

items.s: Your elder brother is involved in immoral activities.
items.r: Talk to him privately, then involve parents and elders to guide him.

items.s: You accidentally killed a person; a woman driving a car thinks she did it.
items.r: Tell the truth to the police and accept responsibility.

items.s: On the way to a job interview you see an injured person.
items.r: Give first aid, take him to hospital, then inform the interviewers and reschedule.

items.s: As mess instructor, your senior tells you to make extra bills.
items.r: Refuse politely and report to higher authority if he insists.

items.s: A stranger follows you and your sister.
items.r: Go to a crowded place, keep her safe and inform the police if needed.

items.s: During COVID you see people stealing basics from a store.
items.r: Stop them politely, inform the owner and help arrange aid for the needy.

items.s: A dog bites you and snatches some meat on the way home.
items.r: Get treatment and a vaccine first; forget the meat.

items.s: You are the only son; parents want you to marry, but marrying makes you ineligible for the army.
items.r: Explain to parents and request them to wait until after commission.

items.s: An old man keeps staring and winking at you.
items.r: Ignore him and move away; inform security if he continues.

items.s: You got a foreign scholarship at PMA but your fitness is not good.
items.r: Accept it and work hard daily to improve fitness.

items.s: Your younger brother uses too much mobile and is failing; he does not listen.
items.r: Set a routine with parents, limit phone time politely and help him with studies.

items.s: You committed a sin; admitting it will defame you.
items.r: Repent sincerely, correct the wrong and make amends; admit where others' rights are involved.

items.s: A girl is stuck in a jungle at night with no way to call police.
items.r: Stay calm, find a safe spot, keep light, move towards a road at daylight.

items.s: A friend calls and says he wants to commit suicide.
items.r: Keep him talking, go to him at once, inform his family and get professional help.

items.s: A friend is addicted to bad deeds and does not listen.

items.s: You are sent on a secret mission but your family stops you.

items.s: Someone steals from a bank and gives it to the poor; you know him.

items.s: A topper cheated while ill; the teacher finds out.

Picture story test is also called TAT (Thematic Apperception Test). It shows your motives, worries and how you see the world.
Usually 3 to 4 pictures. Each picture is shown for about 30 seconds; you get about 3 minutes 30 seconds to write each story (about 16 minutes for 4).
Pictures are black and white and often dim, so observe carefully: ages, number of people, weather, place, mood.
Write about 8 to 10 lines. Think first, then write. Do not just describe the picture; write a story.
Every story needs a hero: a normal person (not a superman) with name, age, job or purpose that matches the picture.
Show what the situation is, what led to it, what the hero does, and the result.
The hero should take help from family, friends, teachers, police, ambulance, doctors or the public; he should not do everything alone.
Implement the plan in action instead of only describing plans. Show small problems that come up and how they are solved.

Story must be positive, practical and complete with a successful ending. Avoid pointless killing or accident themes; if something negative is clearly shown (like an injured person), do not ignore it, handle it.
Do not over-praise the hero at the start and do not give him a big reward at the end.
Use short sentences and simple language. Write neatly.
Qualities seen: observation, judgement, quick decision, emotional balance, confidence, problem solving, handling pressure, communication, cooperation, attitude to life, imagination.

Preparation: write two or three timed stories daily. Practise common themes: road accident, house fire, robbery, purse snatching, a fainted woman, office problems, village and farming. First focus on quality, then build speed, and discuss stories with others.

Sample good themes: a student weak in English practises daily and becomes fluent; a young man chases a snatcher and with public help hands him to police; a student who came last in an essay contest reads daily and wins second place; a farmer notices thieves in a friend's house, calls police and helps catch them.
4 picture stories, about 4 minutes each.
4 picture stories are given, 4 minutes for each story.
Picture story (TAT): about 10-12 pictures/slides; each shown for about 30 seconds, then about 3 minutes to write.
Cover four things: what led to the scene, what is happening now, what the characters think and feel, and the outcome.
Observe the picture closely, including any written words, and identify the main character (hero).
Give simple names to characters.
Keep it about 12 lines / 75 words: roughly equal parts past, present and future.
Avoid negative, defeatist or sad endings; show a confident, positive, action-oriented hero.
Practise at home using everyday scenes.
Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) = picture story writing. About 10-12 vague pictures (slides) are shown one by one.
Look carefully: note any written words, the people in the picture and what they are doing.
Your hero should show planning, leadership, teamwork, helping others and achieving the goal.
Some pictures are clear and some are blurred; write about what you actually see.
This is described as one of the most important psych tests - give the hero a clear role, a problem, positive action and a good result.
Avoid negative themes like sex, death or fights; most candidates add negativity, so stand out with positive stories.

tips: OPI (personality test) had about 150 statements in about 40 minutes.
Options run from Strongly Agree to Strongly Disagree (agree, mostly agree, slightly agree, neutral, slightly disagree, mostly disagree, strongly disagree).
Answer honestly and quickly; many statements repeat in different words to check consistency.
OPI means Occupational Personality Inventory: a list of statements about your preferences and behaviour.
It is like the Big Five personality test and is used to cross-check your other psych tests.
About 150 statements, about 30-40 minutes.
Each statement has 7 options: strongly disagree, mostly disagree, slightly disagree, neutral, slightly agree, mostly agree, strongly agree. Pick only one.
There is no right or wrong answer; ISSB does not want only one type of person (for example, not only extroverts).
Answer honestly. Faking answers to impress creates mismatch with your other tests.
Try not to choose neutral too often; agree or disagree according to your real nature.
Do not get stuck on one statement; keep moving.
You can practise free Big Five / personality tests online to get familiar.
OPI is also called the personality test. You get a booklet of about 150 statements and about 40 minutes to fill a bubble sheet. There is no negative marking.
Each statement has a scale: Strongly Disagree, Mostly Disagree, Slightly Disagree, Neutral, Slightly Agree, Mostly Agree, Strongly Agree (some versions say just Agree/Disagree).
Answer honestly and quickly. Do not overthink one statement; keep a steady pace so you finish all 150.
Many statements repeat the same idea in different words (for example 'I like order' and 'I love order and regularity'). Keep your answers consistent; inconsistency is noticed.

Agree with positive traits you really have (keeping promises, working hard, helping others, following rules, turning plans into action). Disagree with negative traits (panicking easily, losing temper, mood swings, using others, rash decisions).
Do not mark Neutral too often; it shows you cannot make up your mind.
The last few items can be short situation questions with options. Pick the calm, responsible and practical option.
Situation: bus reaches your stop and you have not bought a ticket due to rush. Best: call the conductor, give him the money and get the ticket.
Situation: a child is drowning and you can swim. Best: dive in and save him (while asking others to call for help).
Situation: the exam paper is very tough. Best: stay calm and solve as much as you know with a cool head.
Situation: the host offers one more chapati when you are full. Best: politely say the food was very good but you have already eaten enough.
Situation: a friend has been cheating you. Best: talk to him and make him realise his mistake.
Situation: the lights go out in a dark parking area. Best: stay calm and take help from someone nearby (or wait safely till the lights come back).
Situation: an angry customer wants to meet the senior manager. Best: be patient, calm him down and try to remove his problem by consulting seniors.
A self-esteem style questionnaire may use a 1 to 7 agree/disagree scale; some negative items are reverse scored, so answer honestly and consistently.
Answer how you actually behave, not how you wish you behaved.

tips: The Board Questionnaire (BQ) or Personal Information Questionnaire (PIQ) is filled on arrival and is the most important document; the interview is based on it.

It asks: name (capitals, as in application), batch and chest number, father's name, addresses, district/tehsil, religion, date of birth, parents' education/occupation/income, education record from Matric (marks, division, medium, hostel), number of brothers and sisters and your position, age, height, weight, current occupation and income, NCC training, games and sports, hobbies, extra-curricular activities, positions of responsibility, previous ISSB attempts and previous service.
Write only the truth. Any mismatch between PIQ and interview answers is viewed very seriously.
Be ready to answer questions on everything you write. If you write 'reading' as a hobby, know authors and books you read recently; if you write a sport, know its rules and players.
The PIQ (Personal Information Questionnaire / Board Questionnaire / Biodata) is filled on arrival day and is the most important document you give to ISSB.
The interviewing officer uses it as the base of the interview, so every answer must be true and you must be able to explain it.
If you write a sport (e.g. basketball) you must know it well; if you write 'reading' as a hobby, know authors and books you read recently.
Fields include: name in capitals as in application, father's name, present and permanent address, district/tehsil, religion, date of birth.
Parents'/guardian's education, occupation and income.
Educational record from Matric onwards: year, division, marks, medium, hostel or day scholar.
Number of brothers and sisters, their occupation, and your position among siblings.
Age, height, weight, present occupation and income if any.
NCC training, games and sports, hobbies/interests, extra-curricular activities.
Positions of responsibility held in school, college, sports or other fields.
Details of previous ISSB appearances and previous service, if any.
On the first day the biodata form includes writing about one life event, e.g. 'Aim of my life' or 'Turning point of my life'.
Prepare short, true and positive write-ups for these events in advance.
Even for sad or failure topics, show what you learned and how you recovered.
The bio-data form may ask you to write about one event of your life (see essay topics list). Write honestly and show what you learned from it.
Biodata forms are filled on Reporting Day (from about 3 pm until late evening).

Form asks: height, weight, identification mark, name, father's name, date of birth and age, father's occupation/rank, income, parents' education, brothers and sisters and your position among them, religion, sect, caste, mother tongue, marital status, favourite personality and why.
Previous appearances at ISSB/GHQ with results - hiding them can disqualify you.
Education with marks/grades and prizes; social activities (societies, debates, magazine, position held); games and sports with level and prizes.
Hostel life, foreign travel, type of friends you like, hobbies, place of upbringing (village/town).

What career you will adopt if not selected and why; most unforgettable incident of your life; relatives in the armed forces.
Prepare short positive life-event paragraphs, e.g. turning point of life, happiest moment, aim of life, highest achievement, painful event.

Sample unforgettable moment: being made captain of a team and scoring the winning goal in a final.
Sample unforgettable moment: getting good Matric marks and seeing the proud smile on your father's face.

In the merits and demerits test you write good and bad points about yourself in about 5 minutes.
Write 3 merits and 3 demerits, or 5 and 5.
Write only real points. Remember what you wrote, because you can be asked about it in the interview.
After this test the psych tests are complete and you hand the dossier back to the invigilator.
Choose demerits that are honest but minor and fixable, and show you are working on them.

Example merits: ambitious, confident, courageous, creative, dependable, diligent, empathetic, enthusiastic, hardworking, honest, humble, takes initiative, leadership, loyal, optimistic, patient, persevering, resourceful, responsible, self-disciplined, self-aware, supportive, trustworthy.
Example demerits: shy, procrastinating, easily distracted, impulsive, sensitive, inflexible, perfectionist, introverted, too critical of self, disorganized, indecisive, stubborn, overly competitive.
Self-appraisal shows how well you know your own strengths and weaknesses.
Follow the given structure; do not invent new formats.

Part A - What I think of myself: physical aspects (height, health, fitness, sports), social contacts, education, family and economic status, religion (and respect for all religions), cultural and co-curricular interests, hobbies.
Part B - What others think of me: parents, teachers, friends, opponents ('enemies'), qualities I want to develop, opinion of my boss (if employed).
Do not write too much about physical traits and family.
Be careful about friends: if you are not very social, say you have a few close friends; a wide social circle is best if true.
Do not boast; do not claim strengths you do not have - examiners already know a lot from other tests.
Do not hide weaknesses; mention them tactfully with how you are improving them. Do not describe negatives in detail.
Call opponents 'opponents', not enemies; say you want to be friendly with them.
End by showing willingness to improve. Nobody is perfect.
Your self-description must match what you wrote in other tests and what you say in the interview.
Know your strengths and weaknesses honestly; ask others for honest feedback about how you deal with people.
Show traits like energy, calm temper, flexibility, good listening, fairness, confidence and integrity.
Mention how you are working on a weakness (e.g. practising public speaking, setting goals) instead of only listing it.
Prepare a short, focused self-introduction showing your strengths, achievements and personal qualities.
Keep a record of your school, marks, subjects, best subject, activities, prizes, training, extra skills, appreciation received, newspapers you read, hobby, favourite game and leadership qualities.
Be truthful; anything false will be caught.
The Self-Appraisal test asks you to describe yourself; examiners compare it with your other tests, so be consistent and honest.
Write family income and status truthfully; do not exaggerate.
Do not boast and do not hide weaknesses; mention limitations politely and show you are working to improve them.
Prepare basic facts about yourself before the test.
Use only real and relevant details; avoid useless information.
Know your real strengths and weaknesses: confidence, social skills, motivation, courage and determination.
Strong positive traits to show: openness to new experience, sense of duty (conscientiousness), emotional stability, self-belief, hope and resilience.
Self-description is the last psych test: write your strengths and weaknesses in about 5 minutes.

Common merits: honest, social, punctual, hard working, respectful, good listener, disciplined, confident, brave, loyal to Pakistan and its forces, trustworthy, responsible, adaptable, helpful, organised, calm in difficulty.

Common demerits: weak handwriting, weak English (and working on it), sleeping late, sometimes missing prayers, overeating, a bit talkative, a bit stubborn, too much time on mobile, did not use full academic potential.
Make each merit specific, e.g. 'Cooperative during group tasks', 'Highly motivated during assignments'.
Make demerits specific and honest but not damaging, e.g. 'Talkative with friends', 'Sometimes miss a prayer', 'Poor handwriting', 'Aggressive with overly talkative people'.
Cover different sides: physical, social, education, family background, moral/religious habits, hobbies and activities.
ISSB essay is 30 minutes on the first day. Topics are social, cultural and general awareness matters.
Initial test has 2 short essays (one English, one Urdu), about 5-10 minutes each; one is often a life event (happiest moment, saddest news etc.).
Read the topic carefully, then make a quick mind map or outline on rough paper before writing.
Time plan for 30 minutes: 5-7 min planning, about 3 min introduction (one paragraph, 1/3 page), about 20 min main points (around 1.5 pages), rest for conclusion.

Structure: Introduction (what you understood and what you will cover), Discussion (define topic, its types/causes, who is responsible, effects on society), Way Forward (solutions), Conclusion (3-5 strong sentences).
Use a centred, underlined title in capitals and clear headings with bullet points.
Make points rather than long explanations; write short sentences; keep the reader's level in mind.
Be bold, moderate and suggestive; use your own inner voice.
Write neatly with as few mistakes as possible.
Practise 4-5 essays on different topics within time and get feedback from parents or teachers.
For life-event essays: be truthful, short and readable, describe your feelings, and explain how the event affected you. Prepare a few events in advance.

Sample outline 'Corruption': types (money, moral), causes, who is responsible, effects; way forward: checks and balances, strict punishment, education, less inequality, better salaries, documenting the economy.

Sample outline 'Successful life': types of success (short/long term, differs per person); helpers (right direction, hard work, health, positive attitude, support, Allah's help); obstacles (laziness, fear, low self-belief, wasting time); signs (flexible, curious, courageous, happy at others' success, contentment); conclusion: consistency, dedication, education.

Sample outline 'Co-education': merits (healthy competition, confidence, teamwork, respect); demerits (cultural norms, distraction, rivalry); way forward (co-education at early or university level, good management, awareness).

Sample outline 'Social media and youth': positives (staying in touch, education, business, news); negatives (health, fifth-generation warfare, time wastage, fake news); way forward (awareness, laws, careful use).

Sample outline 'Role of women in development': areas they contribute (health, teaching, banking, agriculture, military); areas lacking; reasons (culture, child care, education, harassment); measures (empowerment, education, respect, equality).
Sample outline 'Wisdom: age or education': wisdom is judgment and good decisions; age gives experience but no guarantee; education links more strongly with wisdom.
Sample outline 'Work from home': pros (flexibility, no commute, family time, tech skills); cons (isolation, low motivation, distractions, burnout); way forward (hybrid system, focus on productivity).
Sample outline 'Elements of good personality': physical, mental, spiritual, social and emotional elements; achieved through effort, balance, education, religion and sports.

tips: The mechanical test uses picture questions about everyday physics: levers, pulleys, gears, balance, liquids, heat, sound and motion.
Each question usually has options A, B and C; C normally means 'equal' or 'no difference'.
Read each question carefully, look at the picture, then pick the best answer.
Some sections show a flat pattern (net) and ask which box or shape it folds into; the pattern always shows the outside surface.
In folding questions, first check the shape and size, then check which faces are shaded.
There is also a numerical section: give answers in simplest form, do rough work on scratch paper.
Work fast and accurately; do not spend long on one question. If not sure, mark your best guess.

Revise basic ideas: gears next to each other turn in opposite directions; more pulleys mean less force but more rope pulled; a longer lever arm needs less force; wider base is more stable; heat, pressure and sound basics.
There is negative marking, so guess carefully.
Questions are simple but conceptual; stay focused.
Tests basic mechanical sense; no special technical study needed.
Many picture questions (about 50 in 20 minutes); work quickly.
Common topics: gears and wheel directions, pulleys, levers, scissors, liquid pressure, centre of gravity, springs, reflected clocks, magnets, electricity, aeroplane turning direction.
Meshed gears turn in opposite directions; a smaller gear makes more turns.
More pulley ropes supporting the load gives more mechanical advantage.
A longer lever arm (force far from the pivot, load near it) makes lifting easier.
Scissors cut better when the object is close to the pivot and handles are long.
Liquid pressure on the bottom depends on depth, not on the jar's width.
An aeroplane turns towards the side of its lower wing.
The mechanical aptitude test checks basic mechanical sense, not special engineering knowledge.
There are many picture questions (about 50 in 20 minutes); work quickly.
Common topics: gears and direction of rotation, pulleys, levers, scissors, weights, pressure, magnets, pendulums, springs, centrifugal force.
The mechanical aptitude test shows diagrams of mechanisms (gears, levers, pulleys etc.) and must be solved in a limited time.
Mechanical aptitude part checks your understanding of simple mechanisms shown in diagrams, in limited time.
Mechanical aptitude tests check understanding of how things work: levers, pulleys, gears, springs, simple circuits and tools.
For military tests questions focus on principles, not long calculations.
Same answer sheet/booklet method: 5 example questions first, then the test.
About 40-50 MCQs in about 15 minutes, based on general physics and movement of mechanical parts.
Questions often repeat; practise with videos and sample papers about one hour daily.

Question types seen in sources: gears and belts, pulleys, levers and seesaws, scissors and hammers, liquid pressure and pumps, springs, bridges and supports, electric switches and circuits, chains and hooks, boats and wind, heat and colour, sound, pendulums, optical illusions, and a short numerical section on lengths.

examples.title: Guard drop before enemy attack
examples.situation: At 6:45 am you learn an enemy attack may come at 10:30; guards must reach sensitive points (airport, power plant, refinery, flyover) before 10:15. You have 2 trucks (20 each) and a helicopter (6), different road speeds, limited helicopter fuel, 5 min loading/unloading.
examples.solution: Send trucks on metalled roads to the far points and use the helicopter for the farthest/most important point within fuel range; calculate each time to finish before 10:15.

examples.title: Convention under curfew
examples.situation: Participants in different hotels/guest houses must reach the convention centre by 8:00 am from 6:00 am; one van of 32, curfew, no police help, set times per stop and road type.
examples.solution: Plan one route collecting from all hotels in the shortest order, avoiding the slow rough road, and check total time is under 2 hours.

examples.title: Football match tickets
examples.situation: Six friends must reach a stadium before gate closes at 3:50 pm but tickets are left in another city; bus, train and service roads with given speeds.
examples.solution: Send 2 friends by train to fetch the tickets and come via service road to the stadium by 3:50; the rest go by bus and taxi and wait at the stadium.

examples.title: Time bomb and jail attack
examples.situation: As police chief at 1:25 pm you learn a bomb on a rail track will explode at 2:10 and terrorists will attack the central jail at 2:30; train can be delayed 20 min, police station and army camp available.
examples.solution: Ask railway to delay the train, send bomb disposal squad from the nearby police station, and call the army for a helicopter to secure the jail area.

examples.title: Railway sabotage, air crash, terrorists and tigress
examples.situation: Leading 10 men with arms and a jeep, one hour available: possible sabotage on railway line 2 km away, air crash 5 km away, terrorists in a village 15 km away, and two women mauled by a tigress in a nearby forest.
examples.solution: Inform police, station masters, hospital and villagers first. Send a man with the jeep to stop the train using a red cloth or flag. With police and medical help, cordon the crash site and move injured to hospital. Mobilise local armed ex-servicemen to surround the village against terrorists. Send an armed man to help the injured women.

examples.title: Hidden treasure
examples.situation: Company commander with 6 men, a rowing boat, rope and a motor boat must recover robbers' treasure hidden in a cave on a hillock across a lake, guarded by 2 men day and night.
examples.solution: Watch the robbers first. Go at night, since daytime will be seen. Commander and two expert men go by motor boat, switch off the engine near the shore and glide in for surprise, while the rest follow in the rowing boat. Catch robbers, hand them to police and treasure to government.

examples.title: Golden idol and government treasure
examples.situation: 8 armed men, a jeep and boats, from 4 pm to 6 pm: stop a golden idol being smuggled from a temple to an airstrip, and save government treasure being looted at a railway station near a village, while preventing sabotage and losses.
examples.solution: Make a plan using time, men and material: split men between the airstrip and the railway station, inform police and authorities, and protect your own men.

examples.title: Railway sabotage, air crash, terrorists and tiger attack
examples.situation: You lead 10 armed men with a jeep and have 1 hour. A railway line may be sabotaged 2 km from the station, a plane has crashed in hills 5 km away, terrorists struck a village 15 km away, and a tigress has injured 2 women in a nearby forest.
examples.solution: First inform station masters, police, hospital and villagers (including ex-servicemen). Send a man in the jeep to stop the train at least 1 km before the sabotage point by waving a red cloth. With police and doctors, cordon off the crash site and move injured to hospital. Use armed local ex-servicemen to surround the village against terrorists. Send an armed man to help the injured women in the forest.

examples.title: Hidden treasure across the lake
examples.situation: You command 6 men with a rowing boat, a motor boat and rope. Robbers have hidden treasure in a cave on a hill across a lake, guarded by 2 men day and night.
examples.solution: Watch the robbers first. Go at night, since by day you will be seen. Leader and 2 skilled men take the motor boat, switch off the engine once it has speed and glide in quietly to surprise the guards, while the rest follow in the rowing boat as backup. Arrest the robbers, hand them to police and give the treasure to the government.

examples.title: Smuggled idol and train robbery
examples.situation: You have 8 armed men, a jeep and boats, from 4 pm to 6 pm. A golden idol is being smuggled from a temple to an airstrip, and robbers are looting government treasure at a railway station near a village.
examples.solution: Make a plan that protects both targets, avoids loss to your own men and equipment, and prevents any sabotage (practice exercise, no model answer given).

examples.title: Bomb on rail track and attack on jail
examples.situation: As police chief at 1:25 pm you learn a time bomb on the track will explode at 2:10 and terrorists will attack the central jail at 2:30. Train can be delayed 20 min; vehicles 130 km/h; army helicopter available.
examples.solution: Ask railway to delay the train 20 minutes, send the bomb disposal squad from the nearby police station to defuse the bomb before 2:10, and call the army camp for a helicopter and troops to secure the jail and clear the area.

examples.title: Dropping troops with two trucks
examples.situation: Two trucks with limited fuel and a helicopter must drop 6 men at 20 km, 12 men at 40 km and 12 more at 60 km within a time limit.
examples.solution: Work out minutes per km from the speed, run the first truck trip by trip (drop and return), track remaining time and fuel, and use the second truck or helicopter only when needed.

examples.title: Rebuild a broken bridge
examples.situation: A bridge on the main road has collapsed. Work must start by 6 am and finish by 5 pm. Two trucks (60 km/h) are at GHQ. Wood is at a sand hill area and cement at a depot on the far side of the loop road.
examples.solution: Send one truck at once for wood and the other for cement on the shortest roads, calculate each arrival time, start the bridge frame as soon as wood arrives, and keep both trucks busy until all material is at the site well before work time.

examples.title: Evacuate guests from a rest house
examples.situation: At 8:30 am you learn terrorists may attack a rest house with 30 guests. Guests must reach police HQ before 6:30 pm. You have 2 vans (5 people each) and 1 bus (30 people) at HQ, a van at a police station, slow rough and hilly roads, a bridge only light vehicles can use, and a 1-hour boat crossing.
examples.solution: Inform the rest house by phone at once. Send the bus by the long highway (it cannot use the bridge) and the vans by the short road over the bridge. Vans bring the first guests fast; the bus brings the rest. Check each trip time with loading and unloading.

examples.title: Tour for 16 visitors
examples.situation: Eight foreign and eight local guests must see a fort, a museum, salt mines, a village, a horse show stadium and a dam between 7 am and 5 pm. You have two vehicles at 60 km/h and short road distances between places.
examples.solution: Split the group by interest or keep one vehicle per group, plan a loop route so no road is repeated, give fixed time at each place, keep lunch near the middle stop and return before 5 pm.

examples.title: City tour for hostel students
examples.situation: Twenty students want to visit a park, museum, village, agri farm, lake and fair. Only one 6-seat bus runs on three routes at fixed times and speed 60 km/h; the hostel is the start and end point.
examples.solution: Make small groups that leave on different bus timings, send each group first to the place it most wants to see, keep a timetable for each route and bring everyone back to the hostel before night.

examples.title: Accident at a bridge near a scout camp
examples.situation: At 10 am, 60 people are injured at a bridge and the road is blocked. Police station has one truck and one van (different speeds and seats). Hospitals A, B, C, D have a few ambulances (2 stretchers or 4 injured each) and are linked by phone.
examples.solution: Phone all hospitals to send ambulances at once, send the van with scouts to give first aid and clear the road, use the truck for lightly injured, send serious cases to the nearest hospitals first and repeat trips until everyone is shifted.

examples.title: Plane crash near a jungle
examples.situation: A plane has crashed at point D; two people are badly hurt and ten have small injuries. You have 12 men, two ambulances (slow on a rough road), a dangerous jungle with snakes and a river. Ammunition from the plane must be moved to two airports and the enemy may attack in two hours.
examples.solution: First give first aid and send the two serious cases by the faster route in ambulances, guard the crash site, move ammunition in the second wave by the safest road, avoid the jungle at night and inform the army for backup before the two-hour limit.

examples.title: Nuclear plant on an island
examples.situation: After a night attack, marines arrested 52 enemy agents at a nuclear plant on an island; two are badly injured. First aid is at a dispensary on the shore. Start 8 am, finish before 12 noon. You have a motor boat (6 people), a helicopter (4 people or 2 stretchers, limited fuel), a bus (25), and a rowing boat (slow). A bridge on the road closes at 10 am.
examples.solution: Send the two injured by helicopter to the dispensary first. Move the agents in batches by motor boat to the shore and then by bus to the city, using the bridge before 10 am. Keep guards with every batch. Use the rowing boat only as back-up.

examples.title: Injured to hospital, then airport
examples.situation: At 9 am there is an accident at point O. You must take the injured to a hospital where a surgeon is available (90 minutes treatment) and then to the airport before 7 pm. You have one van, rivers with ferries (45 minutes in day), and hotels for a meal break.
examples.solution: Reach O quickly, give first aid, choose the hospital with the surgeon even if a little far, use the ferry in daylight, plan a short meal stop near the route and reach the airport with time to spare.

tips: Progressive Group Task on Day 2: group crosses obstacles with given materials; tests team spirit and initiative.
A group crosses 4 obstacles from start line to finish line in 40 minutes, carrying a load and helping material (planks, ballis, ropes).
Out of bounds rule: red-painted structures and ground between start and finish cannot be touched; if a person or item touches, he goes back to the start of that obstacle with the item.
Jump rule: you may not jump distances over about 4 feet (1 metre) in length or height; use helping material.
Group rule: the whole group with all material and load must cross one obstacle before anyone starts the next.
Time rule: all 4 obstacles in 40 minutes; no fixed time for each obstacle.
Use simple engineering: lever (plank on a drum with rope at one end), bridge (plank across two drums), swing (rope tied to a pole or branch), rope as a ladder.
Always tie a rope to the far end of a plank so it can be pulled back after crossing.
Do not panic at the sight of an obstacle; each has many solutions.
Listen to the rules carefully, use all materials, involve all members, and discuss together.
It tests practical problem solving, teamwork, planning, resourcefulness and attitude towards others.
Listen carefully when the GTO explains the rules and follow them exactly.
Look at all the helping material (planks, ropes, ballis, drums) and use it well.
Discuss with all members, listen to everyone's ideas and work together.
Organise men and material so the obstacle is crossed quickly and smoothly.
Actively help the person who is leading at every step.
Show initiative, drive and dash; be ready to take reasonable risk for the group.
Do not waste time being undecided; stay active all the time.
If you touch any red (out of bounds) part, tell the GTO honestly and accept the penalty; go back to the start line yourself.
Usually there are 3-4 obstacles; the whole group must cross one obstacle before moving to the next.
You may jump gaps up to about one metre in length or height; bigger gaps need planks, ballis or ropes.
Ground between start line and finish line and all red-marked parts are out of bounds; the load (casualty/stretcher, sand bag or ammo box) must also be carried across.
All obstacles must usually be finished in about 40 minutes (about 20 minutes per obstacle as a guide).
Simple engineering ideas: plank on a drum with a rope tied at one end makes a lever; plank on two drums makes a bridge; rope tied to a pole or branch makes a swing; rope can be used as a ladder.
Typical material: a 6 foot plank, two ropes about 16 feet long, and a casualty on a stretcher; structures are drums, hanging ropes, a hanging tyre and bench-like platforms.
When the GTO shows you around, study every structure carefully and plan your moves from one structure to the next.
Give your plan first and with confidence when the GTO says start; if the group accepts it, you become the leader.
Once your plan is accepted, give each member a job at once and praise people for good work.
If your plan is not accepted, support the group fully and enthusiastically; this also earns credit.
When the group gets stuck, give logical and positive suggestions.
Once a decision is made, act firmly and quickly; speed is the key word.
Speak clearly and loudly enough; show no tiredness or nervousness.
Never shout at others or lose your temper; accept your mistakes openly.
Choose the right man for the right job and show organising ability.
In PGT the group is given practical obstacles and must carry objects of bulk and weight across them. It is an outdoor task on Day 2.
Follow the set path strictly.
Watch the time limit; speed matters.
Show initiative, zeal, interest and cooperation; show no tiredness or nervousness.
Accept your mistake without excuses; do not avoid responsibility.
The PGT is a set of 3 linked tasks done by the whole group, in about 40 minutes.
Be active, take part in planning, share your ideas and help complete the task.
Cooperate; do not force your ideas on others.
Progressive Group Task is a combination of 3 tasks; time is about 40 minutes.
Jumping and throwing are usually allowed; 2-feet rule usually not applied.
Red areas are out of bound; red-and-white areas are in bound only for materials; other colours (white, yellow, blue) are in bound; the ground is out of bound.
Materials: rope, bamboo, planks (small/large), drums, box, tyre.
All candidates and all materials must cross the finish line in time; nothing should be left behind.
Task language is Urdu but some English is fine; co-operate with group fellows.
If someone touches out of bound, that step is repeated (not from the start in HGT).
No time limit per obstacle, only the total time.
Colour codes (red, blue, yellow, white) mark what is allowed; listen carefully to the instructions.

samples: Sample PGT obstacle: two red-topped drums 6 feet apart, then a 4-foot platform and a hanging rope. Bridge drum to drum with the long plank, slide the short plank onto the platform, send two men over first to receive the load, then use the hanging rope to swing the last man and pull the planks over with a rope.
Sample PGT obstacle: a low wall with a red ditch behind it. Put a plank on the wall as a ramp, form a human chain to pass the load, then lay the plank across the ditch from the top of the wall.

tips: Half Group Task on Day 2: done in a smaller half group so each member gets more chance to show initiative.
The group is split into two halves (about 4 each); each half faces one obstacle separately.
Usually one obstacle, about 10-15 minutes allowed.
You must carry a load (like a drum) plus helping material (balli, rope, plank) from start line to finish line.
Area between start and finish line and anything painted red is out of bounds for men, load and material.
Fewer people means everyone must work and contribute; it is still a group task, so cooperate.
GTO first tells the requirement, the helping material and the rules, then clears doubts before you start.
Example: one half swings the drum across using a rope loop from the middle structure while the plank bridges the gaps between the fixed drums and the structure.
After the first half finishes, the second half crosses in its own best way.
HGT is like PGT but with half the group, so each person gets more chance to show ideas. Held on Day 2.
The Half Group Task is done with half of the group, after the Snake Race.
The group (usually 8 to 10) is split into two halves; each half does one obstacle separately.
Time is usually 10 to 15 minutes. Rules are the same as other group tasks.
Usually you must carry a load like a drum from start line to finish line using helping material such as ballis, rope and plank.
Fewer people means everyone must put a hand to the work; it is still a group task, so cooperate.
The GTO explains the requirement, the material and the rules, then answers doubts before you start.
Sample solution: bridge the gaps between fixed drums with the plank, send two men across, keep one man on top of the middle structure to swing the drum across in a rope loop, then the rest cross.
After the first half finishes, the second half crosses in its own way.
The group is split into two sub-groups; there is no commander.
Each sub-group must cross a set area with hurdles and out-of-bound places.
In the Half Group Task the group is split into two sub-groups with no commander; you cross an area with obstacles and out-of-bound places.
Group is divided into 2-4 sub-groups; each half group gets a different task.
Same rules as PGT; time about 10 minutes per sub-group.
If you touch out of bound, you redo from the previous step, not from the start.
Half/semi group task: the group is split into 3-4 small groups, each doing a different task in about 10 minutes.
Same rules as the progressive group task; Urdu may be spoken.

samples: Sample HGT obstacle: one drum in the middle of a red area with a tall pole on the far side. Lay the plank start-line to drum, tie a rope loop to the pole, swing the load across on the rope, then shift the plank from drum to finish line.

tips: Each command task has a start line, finish line, inbound (usable) and out-of-bound (red) areas, ditches, drums, and planks of different sizes.
Read the conditions on the board: usually jumping and throwing are not allowed; in some tasks jumping is allowed but throwing is not.
Do not step in out-of-bound (red) areas; use drums and planks as supports and bridges.
When you are the commander, start with a short clear briefing (situation, mission, how, who does what, control) and give jobs to each helper.
You may appoint a time-keeper to remind you of time; time limit is there to create pressure, good teamwork matters more.
Use a cantilever (weight on one end of a plank) when gaps are too long for one plank.
Keep all helpers involved and keep the load in contact with a support while moving (chain method).
Sample idea - canyon crossing: cross a roped area using planks and drums placed at uneven distances.
Sample idea - retrieval: lift an object from a no-entry area with two long ropes by twisting them around it and pulling tight.
Sample idea - silent bomb carry: carry a load over obstacles keeping it level with hand signals only.
Sample idea - casualty evacuation: follow known safe tracks, pass the casualty carefully, make a stretcher from two poles and jackets.
Sample idea - river stones: cross on drums; each drum is removed once nobody touches it, so move as a chain and help blindfolded members.
On Day 3 each candidate in turn is made commander and given a practical task needing several men.
Plan quickly, give clear orders, use helpers well and stay calm.
Give clear instructions and explain the reason; let members find their own way and help where needed rather than imposing every detail.
Value ideas from your team and give quick feedback.
Stay calm and even-tempered; your attitude affects the whole group.
Each candidate in turn becomes commander; the GTO gives him an obstacle.
The commander chooses 3-4 candidates of his choice as helpers; choose active, energetic and cooperative boys.
Time is short, usually about 5-10 minutes; material is usually a plank, 1-2 ropes, maybe a pole or small ladder; load is usually an ammunition box.
Make a quick, practical plan keeping men, material and time in mind; then brief your men clearly step by step.
Give each man a clear job; make sure nobody stands idle.
Mainly supervise; do not do all the work yourself, but help when someone is in difficulty.
Stand where you can watch the whole work.
Do not keep asking subordinates for ideas; but if your plan fails, stay calm and take a suggestion in a dignified way.
Do not shout, mumble or be harsh; look smart and command in a firm, measured tone.
When you are a subordinate, follow the commander's orders sincerely and loyally; the GTO also judges you as a helper.
Same rules as other group tasks (red is out of bounds).
The Command Task is part of the outdoor GTO series, done after Individual Obstacles.
As commander you lead the group through an area with hurdles and out-of-bound parts.
When you are commander, the GTO may also ask a short interview about your activities, studies and family.
The GTO may ask the commander questions: ISSB performance, quick maths, life, academic record.
Commander gets about 2 minutes to plan, then calls the group (he may choose helpers), briefs them on task, materials, rules and plan.
Jumping and throwing are not allowed; 2-feet rule applies (no step longer than a normal step).
If time ends, the GTO may ask the commander to explain his plan; a correct plan counts.
Only the commander plans; others must obey him. As a subordinate, cooperate fully with the commander.
Ask your helpers for ideas, but take the decision yourself.
Do not give up even if you do not understand the task; keep trying.
On the way to the task, the GTO talks with you frankly like a short interview.
Plan, give clear brief orders, supervise from a good position and keep everyone busy.
Avoid doing all the work yourself; help only when needed.
Urdu may be spoken.

tips: Simple individual obstacles done on Day 3 to test courage, stamina and determination.
Wear tracksuit; no jewellery.
There are about 10 individual obstacles, done alone, usually within about 3 minutes.
Each obstacle carries marks equal to its number (No. 1 = 1 mark, No. 10 = 10 marks); harder ones give more marks.
You do not have to go in serial order; start with the ones you are confident about.
IO tests agility, physical toughness, boldness, courage, determination, stamina and speed.
Listen carefully when the GTO explains each obstacle and judge which are easy for you.
Do not leave an obstacle half done unless you really cannot do it; if you fail, try again.
Keep an eye on time and try to finish within it.
Practice: daily free-hand exercise, running, skipping, parallel bars, rings and beam (with someone nearby for safety); toughen up gradually and do not overdo.
Rope climbing: use hands, feet and knees with a firm grip.
Long jump over ditch: do not look into the ditch; look at the other side and go fast.
Monkey crawl: use hands and feet, keep head higher than the rope, move hands and feet alternately, do not look down.
Tarzan swing: catch the rope as high as possible, hold firmly, swing and let go at the farthest point, then land confidently.
Passing through tyre: hold the rope above the tyre firmly and slide through legs first.
Wall climbing: jump and get up with a sudden push, keep your momentum.
Plank jump: run up the sloping board, keep balance on the small plank, then jump to the next plank.
Parallel ropes: climb up the rope ladder, stand on the lower rope, hold the upper rope and slide hands and feet along with balance.
Tarzan jump: run up about 40-50 yards and jump freely.

Start in the starting circle and begin on the whistle; stop on the second whistle.

Red-painted parts are out of bound.

tips: GTO tests put candidates in standard situations to judge officer-like qualities: team spirit, initiative, cooperation and leadership.
In group tasks, cooperate, encourage others and stay positive even when the task fails; courage and resilience are being judged.
The GTO explains the load, materials, out-of-bounds areas and every obstacle before starting; clear all doubts before you begin.
Outdoor tests check leadership, intelligence, initiative, original ideas, planning, self-confidence and cooperation.
Snake Race (Inter-Group Obstacle Race): four groups race side by side over similar obstacles, carrying a casualty/stretcher (often a bamboo with a tent tied).
Snake race tests fitness, courage, determination, cooperation and team spirit in a leaderless group.
In the snake race the team result counts, so help weaker members.
Take maximum responsibility and effort; do not hesitate to take risks; show dash and determination.
Do not show off; the GTO will notice your work anyway. Do not lose heart if your team is not first.
Snake race rules and penalties are the same as in PGT.

Snake race obstacle examples: three vertical structures (two cross first, two sit on the middle to pass the casualty); two ballis joined by a swinging plank bridge; an 8 foot plastered wall with a rope net on top.
GTO tests put candidates in standard situations to see officer-like qualities such as team spirit, initiative, courage and leadership.

Take as much responsibility and effort on yourself as you can; take risks without hesitation.
Show dash and determination, but do not show off; the GTO will notice your work anyway.
Do not lose heart even if your group does not come first.
Rules and penalties are the same as in the Progressive Group Task.

2-feet rule: you cannot take a step longer than a normal step unless jumping is allowed.
'No throwing' means pass materials hand to hand.
Mutual Assessment: after all tasks, rank your group fellows by performance (write their chest numbers in order) honestly and fairly; it checks your judgement.

Practice task example: 6 candidates, two planks and a box, ground out of bound, no jumping/throwing - build plank bridges step by step, use the box as a support, and move people and materials forward together.
Materials are rope, bamboo, small and large planks, small and big drums, box and tyre.
Do not look at the GTO during tasks; focus on the task.
Do not act artificially to look efficient; the GTO is experienced. Over-acting can harm you.
The GTO looks for people who perform best under pressure.
Wear white shirt, white shorts, white socks and white canvas shoes for physical tasks.
Physical fitness is a must; daily running, sit-ups and exercise for about 45 minutes.
Watch videos of command and group tasks to understand them.
Interview is said to be judged mostly on body language and tone, then on words; sit straight, keep eye contact and speak calmly.
Expect deep questions on your family: parents' background and jobs, siblings, family income, grandfather's job.
Expect academic questions: favourite and weak subjects, matric and inter marks and percentage, school address, reasons for any failure.
Expect self-analysis and stress questions (relationships, lying, what if rejected); answer honestly and calmly.
Quick mental maths on speed, distance, time and percentages is common.
Revise physics laws from 9th-12th class (Newton's laws, Boyle's law, Charles's law, resonance).
Know Pakistan's borders (Durand Line, Pak-China, Pak-India border lengths), religious basics, common abbreviations and the armed forces (ranks, chiefs, Nishan-e-Haider holders).
The Deputy President may ask personal, tricky or even provocative questions to test your honesty, morals and calmness. Stay polite, calm and firm; never lose your temper.
Be ready to explain weak grades honestly and to say what you will do if not recommended (try again with more preparation).
Know the Pakistan Army motto: Iman, Taqwa, Jihad fi Sabilillah.
Simple mental maths can be asked.
Expect personal, family and odd questions; answer calmly and honestly.
Questions may come from your field of study and your hobby, so know them well.
Expect quick mental maths questions.
Start 'Tell me about yourself' with the present and what makes you fit for the forces; do not ramble about your whole life.
Keep a mental list of your strengths with one real example each.
For weaknesses, stay positive and show how you are working to improve; never give a damaging fault.
Do not badmouth anyone (school, teachers, family, previous place). Never be negative.
Never lie; it is easily checked.
If the interviewer stays silent after your answer, stay calm; do not ramble. Politely ask if he wants more detail.
For regrets, show you are positive and learned from your experiences.
Show you can work under pressure with a real example.
For 'what makes you angry', show you are calm and even-tempered; dishonesty or laziness can annoy you.
Have a few role models ready and say what you learned from them.
Prepare examples of your toughest decision and toughest challenge: why it was hard, what you did, result.
If you are pressured to choose between loyalty and honesty, choose honesty/integrity.
Stay confident and calm with stress questions like 'you are not fit for this'; answer politely with reasons.
Speak clearly at a steady pace in a firm voice; slow speech shows calm, fast speech shows nervousness.
Keep eye contact; do not look away or close your eyes while talking.
Sit still; do not fidget with hair, pen or watch.
Admit mistakes honestly and explain what you learned from them.
Sit naturally and comfortably, not stiff; sit straight and lean slightly forward.
If you do not know, say 'Sorry sir, I don't know'; never bluff.
Speak clearly and confidently at a normal speed and volume; nervous people speak too fast.
Avoid mannerisms: no fidgeting, touching face or nose, rubbing neck, shaking legs, folded arms or slouching.
Keep your head up, shoulders relaxed and hands calm; use hands only a little to explain.
Dress neatly: clean pressed clothes, polished shoes, proper haircut.
Be honest, confident and well-dressed (shalwar qameez or shirt-trousers in summer; suit/combination in winter) with proper haircut and shave.
Know your reasons for joining the forces and be updated on current and defence affairs.
Knock, wait to be called in, greet the officer, and sit only when asked; say thank you.
Do not offer your hand first for a handshake; if a handshake happens, keep it firm with eye contact.
When finished, say thank you and leave, putting the chair back in place.
Know common abbreviations (e.g. NADRA, ISPR, PEMRA, OGRA, NEPRA, NLC, FWO, NHA, OIC, ECO, SAARC, UNICEF, WHO, IMF, NATO).
Mostly Urdu, but you can use English.
Remember the position you claim in GTO tasks; keep your answers consistent.

Learn GK basics: intelligence agencies (ISI Pakistan 1948, RAW India 1968, Mossad Israel 1949, CIA USA 1947, MI6 UK 1909, MSS China 1983, BND Germany 1956), titles of prophets and companions, Islamic battles (Badr 2 AH, Uhud 3 AH, Khandaq 5 AH, Hudaibiya 6 AH, Khyber 7 AH, Mutah 8 AH, Conquest of Makkah 8 AH, Tabuk 9 AH, Farewell Hajj 10 AH, Karbala 61 AH).

Confidence is more important than knowledge; if you do not know, say so and move on.
Speak naturally and clearly, avoid slang, do not bluff, do not argue, stick to your view politely.
Zakat on an amount = amount / 40 (e.g. Rs 2400 -> Rs 60). Amount from zakat = zakat x 40.
Poles needed = (length / gap) + 1; length needed = (poles - 1) x gap.

tips: Psychologist looks at self-confidence, self-efficacy, sociability, assertiveness, courage and determination; prepare real-life examples of each.
Show you can handle criticism calmly and that you take responsibility for your actions.
Show balanced assertiveness: you can say no politely and give your opinion without being rude or bossy.
Psychological questions check sociability, assertiveness, motivation, courage and self-confidence; answer honestly.
Show you can make friends easily, mix with new people and help others.
Show you can say no politely and give clear reasons.
Show you set goals, keep trying after failure and stay positive.
The psychologist also interviews you; be natural, honest and positive.
The Psychologist also takes an interview; be honest and consistent with what you wrote in your tests and forms.

The psychologist compares your psych tests and forms with your personality.
Some questions are negative or provocative on purpose; answer in a calm, positive and decent way.

He compares your psych tests and forms with your personality, so be consistent with what you wrote.

He may ask about characters you named in your stories (e.g. who is the girl in your story).
The interview is done by an expert psychologist; sometimes an observer sits in to watch your expressions. The psychologist can be male or female; do not react.
Candidates wait in a lounge; a light above the door blinks for 1-2 seconds when it is your turn. Do not miss it.
It usually lasts 5-10 minutes, sometimes up to 20.

Usual order of topics: expression, daily activities, friends, your test sentences, ideal personality, logical questions, merits and demerits, events of life, sex-related questions, emotional questions.
Enter with a confident face and a mild smile; shake hands only if he offers.
Sit only when allowed; do not look around the room or at pictures and items.
Do not complain about ISSB life.
Friends: say a normal number (around 10-12 good friends, 1 close friend), not social media friends, and not zero.
Do not sit until you are asked to.
Do not look at the pictures on the walls or items on the table; stay focused on the psychologist.
Wear formal dress, be presentable and use a mild cologne.
Speak clearly in the language you are comfortable with (English or Urdu).
Stick to what you wrote in WAT/SCT; questions are asked from your test answers.
Tell a real weakness honestly; nobody is perfect.
If you do not know an answer, say sorry politely instead of making things up.
Do not blame the government or officials.
Focuses on your mind, fears, ambitions and ideals, not academics.
Give the same answers you gave the Deputy; being truthful makes this easy.
If the psychologist is a lady, be respectful, formal and keep normal eye contact.
Questions about friends of the opposite sex or marriage may come; answer normally.
